questions.stem: Which of the following is a fundamental quantity?
questions.explanation: The seven SI base quantities include length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity; the others are derived.

questions.stem: Which of these SI units is derived from base units rather than being a base unit itself?
questions.explanation: The joule is kg m^2 s^(-2), built from base units; the mole, candela and second are among the seven SI base units.

questions.stem: The dimensions of pressure are
questions.explanation: Pressure = force/area = (M L T^(-2))/L^2 = M L^(-1) T^(-2).

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs has the same dimensions?
questions.explanation: Work (force x distance) and torque (force x perpendicular distance) are both M L^2 T^(-2).

questions.stem: The most suitable instrument for measuring the diameter of a thin wire is a
questions.explanation: A micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm, the precision needed for a thin wire.

questions.stem: Vernier calipers are best suited for measuring the
options: thickness of a sheet of paper
internal diameter of a test tube
questions.explanation: Vernier calipers have jaws for internal and external diameters and read to 0.01 cm (0.1 mm).

questions.stem: On a micrometer screw gauge the sleeve reading is 2.5 mm and the 38th thimble division is in line with the datum line. If each thimble division is 0.01 mm, what is the reading?
The dimension of the gravitational constant G (from F = G m1 m2 / r^2) is
The SI unit of power expressed in base units is
questions.explanation: Power = energy/time = (kg m^2 s^(-2))/s = kg m^2 s^(-3).

questions.stem: The beam balance measures mass, rather than weight, because it
options: uses a spring that stretches with weight
measures the pull of the earth directly
compares the unknown mass with standard masses under the same gravity
questions.explanation: Both pans experience the same g, so g cancels when the moments balance.

questions.stem: A device suitable for timing a 100 m race is a
questions.explanation: A stopwatch can be started and stopped manually and reads to fractions of a second.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and direction; the others have magnitude only.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement, so it has no direction.

questions.stem: Two forces of 9 N and 12 N act at right angles on a body. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
Two forces, each of magnitude 5 N, act at a point with an angle of 60 degrees between them. Find their resultant.
A force of 40 N acts at 30 degrees above the horizontal. Find its vertical component.
questions.explanation: Vertical component = 40 sin 30 = 20 N; the horizontal component is 40 cos 30 = 34.64 N.

questions.stem: A canoe is paddled at 4 m/s straight across a river flowing at 3 m/s. What is the resultant velocity of the canoe relative to the bank?
questions.explanation: The two velocities are perpendicular, so v = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: Two cars travel in the same direction along a straight road at 80 km/h and 65 km/h. What is the velocity of the faster car relative to the slower one?
options: -15 km/h in the direction of motion
questions.explanation: For motion in the same direction, relative velocity = 80 - 65 = 15 km/h forward.

questions.stem: Two trains approach each other on parallel tracks at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. What is the speed of one relative to the other?
questions.explanation: When moving towards each other the speeds add: 50 + 70 = 120 km/h.

questions.stem: Forces of 8 N due east and 6 N due north act on a particle. Find the direction of their resultant measured from east.
questions.explanation: tan(theta) = 6/8, so theta = 36.9 degrees north of east (the resultant is 10 N).

questions.stem: The maximum and minimum resultants of two forces of 7 N and 4 N are
questions.explanation: The resultant is greatest (7 + 4) when the forces act together and least (7 - 4) when they act in opposite directions.

questions.stem: The motion of the pendulum bob of a wall clock is an example of
questions.explanation: The bob moves to and fro about a fixed (equilibrium) position.

questions.stem: The movement of smoke particles seen under a microscope is an example of
questions.explanation: Smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by air molecules and move in a zig-zag, unpredictable way (Brownian motion).

questions.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s^2 for 8 s. Find its final velocity.
A cyclist moving at 5 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s^2 for 6 s. How far does she travel in this time?
A lorry moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest in a distance of 50 m. Find its deceleration.
questions.explanation: v^2 = u^2 + 2as gives 0 = 400 + 100a, so a = -4 m/s^2; the deceleration is 4 m/s^2.

questions.stem: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a speed of 30 m/s. Find the maximum height reached. (g = 10 m/s^2)
A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 30 m/s. How long does it take to return to the thrower's hand? (g = 10 m/s^2; ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: The time to the top is u/g = 3 s, and the descent takes the same time: 6 s in total.

questions.stem: A stone is dropped from the top of a building 80 m high. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: h = (1/2)gt^2 gives t = sqrt(2 x 80/10) = 4 s.

questions.stem: A stone dropped from rest falls 80 m to the ground. With what speed does it hit the ground? (g = 10 m/s^2)
The slope of a distance-time graph gives the
questions.explanation: Gradient = change in distance/change in time = speed.

questions.stem: The area under a velocity-time graph represents the
questions.explanation: Area = velocity x time = displacement.

questions.stem: A bus accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 4 s, moves at 12 m/s for 6 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3 s. Find the total distance covered.
For a bus that accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 4 s, cruises for 6 s and stops uniformly in 3 s, what is the deceleration in the last stage?
questions.explanation: Deceleration = 12/3 = 4 m/s^2 (the gradient of the final section of the v-t graph).

questions.stem: A projectile is fired with a speed of 40 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Find its horizontal range. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: R = u^2 sin 2(theta)/g = 1600 sin 60/10 = 80 sqrt(3), about 138.6 m.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Find the maximum height reached. (g = 10 m/s^2)
A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Find its time of flight on level ground. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: T = 2u sin(theta)/g = 2 x 20/10 = 4 s.

questions.stem: Find the force needed to give a car of mass 1200 kg an acceleration of 2.5 m/s^2.
A girl of mass 60 kg stands in a lift accelerating upwards at 2 m/s^2. Find the reaction of the floor on her. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: R - mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 x 12 = 720 N.

questions.stem: A girl of mass 60 kg stands in a lift accelerating downwards at 2 m/s^2. What reading would a bathroom scale under her show, in newtons? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: mg - R = ma, so R = m(g - a) = 60 x 8 = 480 N.

questions.stem: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley and they move off together. Find their common velocity.
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: 3 x 4 = (3 + 1)v, so v = 3 m/s.

questions.stem: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet with a muzzle speed of 400 m/s. Find the recoil speed of the rifle.
questions.explanation: Total momentum stays zero: 4v = 0.02 x 400 = 8, so v = 2 m/s.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 30 m/s. Find the magnitude of the impulse on the ball.
questions.explanation: Impulse = change in momentum = 0.5(30 - (-20)) = 25 N s; the reversal of direction must be included.

questions.stem: A 150 g cricket ball moving at 40 m/s is stopped by a fielder in 0.01 s. Find the average force on the ball.
questions.explanation: F = change in momentum/time = (0.15 x 40)/0.01 = 600 N.

questions.stem: A stone tied to a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 3 m at a constant speed of 6 m/s. Find its centripetal acceleration.
questions.explanation: a = v^2/r = 36/3 = 12 m/s^2, directed towards the centre.

questions.stem: Find the period of a simple pendulum of length 0.9 m. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) = 2 pi sqrt(0.09) = 0.6 pi, about 1.88 s.

questions.stem: A body performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 4 cm and period 0.5 s. Find its maximum speed.
questions.explanation: v(max) = A(omega) = 0.04 x (2 pi/0.5) = 0.16 pi, about 0.503 m/s.

questions.stem: Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of
questions.explanation: The first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts, which describes inertia.

questions.stem: A passenger standing in a bus jerks backwards when the bus suddenly starts. This is explained by
questions.explanation: The passenger's body tends to remain at rest while the bus (and her feet) move forward.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 0.4 m turns at 300 revolutions per minute. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim.
questions.explanation: v = (2 pi r) x (revolutions per second) = 2 pi (0.4)(5) = 4 pi, about 12.6 m/s.

questions.stem: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
options: one quarter of its original value
questions.explanation: F is proportional to 1/r^2, and (1/2)^2 = 1/4.

questions.stem: Calculate the gravitational force between two masses of 50 kg and 80 kg placed 2 m apart. (G = 6.67 x 10^(-11) N m^2 kg^(-2))
The weight of an astronaut on the Moon is less than on the Earth because
options: the acceleration due to gravity on the Moon is smaller
there is no air on the Moon
the Moon rotates faster than the Earth
questions.explanation: Mass stays the same; weight = mg and g on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on Earth.

questions.stem: A rock weighs 120 N on the Moon, where g is one-sixth of its value on Earth. What is its mass? (g on Earth = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: g on the Moon = 10/6 m/s^2, so m = 120/(10/6) = 72 kg. The mass is the same everywhere.

questions.stem: Estimate the escape velocity from the Earth's surface, given that g = 10 m/s^2 and the Earth's radius is 6.4 x 10^6 m.
questions.explanation: v = sqrt(2gR) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 6.4 x 10^6) = 11314 m/s, about 11.3 km/s.

questions.stem: The value of g at the equator is slightly less than at the poles mainly because
options: the equator is farther from the Earth's centre and the Earth rotates
there is more air at the equator
the magnetic field is weaker at the equator
questions.explanation: The equatorial radius is larger and the rotational effect is greatest at the equator, both reducing g there.

questions.stem: Astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless because
options: there is no gravity in space
the spacecraft is outside the Earth's atmosphere
they and the spacecraft are falling freely together towards the Earth
questions.explanation: Both the astronaut and the craft have the same acceleration (g at that height), so the floor exerts no reaction force.

questions.stem: A satellite in a parking (geostationary) orbit has a period of
questions.explanation: It must turn with the Earth to stay above the same point, so its period equals one day.

questions.stem: The gravitational potential at a point in a gravitational field is
options: always zero at the Earth's surface
independent of distance from the mass
questions.explanation: Taking zero at infinity, V = -GM/r; work must be done to move a mass away, so V is negative near the mass.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a conservative force field?
questions.explanation: Work done in a gravitational field depends only on the start and end points, not the path.

questions.stem: At what value is the acceleration due to gravity at a height equal to the Earth's radius above the surface? (g at the surface = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: g is proportional to 1/r^2; at height R the distance from the centre is 2R, so g = 10/4 = 2.5 m/s^2.

questions.stem: A body is in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar forces. Which of the following must be true?
options: The body must be at rest on the ground
The resultant force on it is zero
questions.explanation: For equilibrium the vector sum of the forces (and the sum of moments) must be zero.

questions.stem: A uniform metre rule is pivoted at its centre. A 40 N weight hangs 30 cm to the left of the pivot. Where must a 60 N weight hang to balance it?
options: 45 cm to the right of the pivot
20 cm to the right of the pivot
30 cm to the right of the pivot
20 cm to the left of the pivot
questions.explanation: Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: 60x = 40 x 30, so x = 20 cm on the other side.

questions.stem: A uniform metre rule balances horizontally on a knife-edge at the 40 cm mark when a 50 g mass hangs at the 10 cm mark. Find the mass of the rule.
questions.explanation: The rule's weight acts at the 50 cm mark, 10 cm from the pivot: m x 10 = 50 x 30, so m = 150 g.

questions.stem: A uniform plank 6 m long and weighing 600 N rests on supports at its ends A and B. A 300 N load is placed 2 m from A. Find the reaction at A.
questions.explanation: Moments about A: 6 R(B) = 600 x 3 + 300 x 2 = 2400, so R(B) = 400 N and R(A) = 900 - 400 = 500 N.

questions.stem: The moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the
options: time for which the force acts
perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
questions.explanation: Moment = F x d, where d is measured perpendicular to the line of action.

questions.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 8 N act on a steering wheel at opposite ends of a diameter of 25 cm. Find the moment of the couple.
questions.explanation: Torque of a couple = one force x perpendicular distance between them = 8 x 0.25 = 2 N m.

questions.stem: A 50 N picture hangs from a nail by two strings, each making 30 degrees with the vertical. Find the tension in each string.
questions.explanation: Resolving vertically: 2T cos 30 = 50, so T = 50/sqrt(3) = 28.9 N.

questions.stem: Lami's theorem states that, for three forces in equilibrium acting at a point, each force is proportional to the
options: cosine of the angle between the other two forces
square of the other two forces
sine of the angle between the other two forces
sum of the other two forces
questions.explanation: F1/sin(alpha) = F2/sin(beta) = F3/sin(gamma), where each angle is between the other two forces.

questions.stem: A body is said to be in stable equilibrium if, when slightly displaced, it
options: moves further away from its original position
questions.explanation: In stable equilibrium the centre of gravity rises on displacement, giving a restoring moment.

questions.stem: A racing car is built with a low, wide base mainly to
options: reduce its centre of mass speed
questions.explanation: A low centre of gravity and wide base make the car harder to topple.

questions.stem: A 30 N weight hanging from a string is pulled aside by a horizontal force F until the string makes 45 degrees with the vertical. Find F.
questions.explanation: Vertically T cos 45 = 30 and horizontally T sin 45 = F, so F = 30 tan 45 = 30 N.

questions.stem: The equilibrant of a system of forces is the single force that
options: has the same direction as the resultant
is the sum of the magnitudes of the forces
is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant
questions.explanation: Adding the equilibrant to the system gives zero resultant.

questions.stem: A force of 50 N pulls a box 8 m along level ground. If the force acts at 60 degrees to the horizontal, find the work done.
questions.explanation: W = Fd cos(theta) = 50 x 8 x 0.5 = 200 J.

questions.stem: Find the kinetic energy of a car of mass 1500 kg moving at 20 m/s.
A 25 kg bag of cement is lifted onto a roof 12 m high. Find the gain in potential energy. (g = 10 m/s^2)
A ball is released from rest at a height of 5 m. Neglecting air resistance, find its speed just before it hits the ground. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: mgh = (1/2)mv^2 gives v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.

questions.stem: A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs 9 m high in 12 s. Find her average power. (g = 10 m/s^2)
A car engine exerts a forward force of 2000 N while the car moves at a steady 15 m/s. Find the power developed.
The force on a body increases uniformly from 0 to 8 N over the first 0.5 m and then stays at 8 N until the displacement is 1.2 m. Find the total work done.
questions.explanation: Work = area under the force-distance graph = (1/2)(0.5)(8) + 8(0.7) = 2 + 5.6 = 7.6 J.

questions.stem: The energy conversion in a battery-powered torch is
options: chemical to electrical to light (and heat)
questions.explanation: The cell converts stored chemical energy to electrical energy, which the bulb converts to light and heat.

questions.stem: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy
options: can neither be created nor destroyed but can be changed from one form to another
is conserved only in elastic collisions
questions.explanation: Total energy in an isolated system remains constant.

questions.stem: The bob of a pendulum passes through its lowest point at 4 m/s. Neglecting air resistance, how high above the lowest point does it rise? (g = 10 m/s^2)
A 2 kg body falls from rest through 20 m and reaches the ground at 18 m/s. How much energy is lost to air resistance? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: PE lost = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 J; KE gained = 0.5 x 2 x 324 = 324 J; difference = 76 J.

questions.stem: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of
questions.explanation: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J, an amount of energy.

questions.stem: If the speed of a moving body is doubled, its kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: KE is proportional to v^2, and 2^2 = 4.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Wind is continually replenished by the sun's heating of the atmosphere; fossil fuels take millions of years to form.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-renewable energy source?
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel; once used it cannot be replaced on a human time scale.

questions.stem: The greenhouse effect is mainly caused by gases such as carbon dioxide which
options: trap long-wavelength infrared radiation emitted by the Earth
block ultraviolet rays from the sun
reflect visible light back into space
absorb sound waves in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Short-wave sunlight passes through, but the re-radiated long-wave infrared is absorbed by greenhouse gases, warming the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Oil spillage in the Niger Delta is an example of
options: an environmental impact of energy production
questions.explanation: Spillage damages farmland, water and fisheries; it is a harmful side-effect of producing energy resources.

questions.stem: Energy diversification in a country means
options: using only the cheapest energy source
relying on several different sources of energy
questions.explanation: Using a mix of sources (hydro, gas, solar, wind) reduces the risk of energy crises.

questions.stem: Burning fossil fuels contributes to global warming mainly by releasing
questions.explanation: Combustion of coal, oil and gas releases CO2, a major greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy is
questions.explanation: A generator uses electromagnetic induction to turn rotational (mechanical) energy into electrical energy; a motor does the reverse.

questions.stem: In a hydroelectric power station, the energy changes are mainly
options: chemical energy to heat to electrical energy
nuclear energy to heat to electrical energy
electrical energy to kinetic energy to potential energy
potential energy to kinetic energy to electrical energy
questions.explanation: Water stored at height loses potential energy as it falls, turning turbines whose kinetic energy drives generators.

questions.stem: A good site for a hydroelectric dam is one that has
options: a large, steady flow of water and a large difference in height
questions.explanation: Power available depends on the flow rate and the head (height through which the water falls).

questions.stem: Water flows at 20 m^3 per second through the turbines of a dam with a head of 50 m. If the plant is 80% efficient, find its electrical power output. (density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: Input power = (mass per second) x g x h = 20,000 x 10 x 50 = 10 MW; output = 0.8 x 10 = 8 MW.

questions.stem: The Kainji and Jebba power stations on the River Niger produce electricity from
questions.explanation: They are hydroelectric stations using water stored behind dams.

questions.stem: In a nuclear power station, energy is released mainly by
options: nuclear fission of heavy nuclei such as uranium-235
fusion of hydrogen in the reactor core
questions.explanation: Fission of U-235 nuclei releases large amounts of energy as heat, which raises steam to drive turbines.

questions.stem: Calculate the energy released if 1 g of matter is completely converted into energy. (c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s)
questions.explanation: E = mc^2 = 0.001 x (3.0 x 10^8)^2 = 9.0 x 10^13 J; forgetting to convert grams to kilograms gives 9.0 x 10^16 J.

questions.stem: The function of the moderator (e.g. graphite) in a nuclear reactor is to
questions.explanation: Slow (thermal) neutrons are more likely to cause fission of U-235; control rods, not the moderator, absorb neutrons.

questions.stem: Control rods in a nuclear reactor are usually made of boron or cadmium because these materials
questions.explanation: Lowering the rods absorbs neutrons and slows the chain reaction.

questions.stem: A major disadvantage of nuclear power is
options: the emission of large amounts of carbon dioxide
the low amount of energy per kilogram of fuel
the production of long-lived radioactive waste
questions.explanation: Spent fuel stays radioactive for a very long time and must be stored safely.

questions.stem: A solar panel (photovoltaic panel) converts
options: light energy directly into electrical energy
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells produce an emf when light falls on them.

questions.stem: The surface of a flat-plate solar water heater is painted dull black because dull black surfaces
options: are poor emitters and poor absorbers
are good absorbers of radiant heat
questions.explanation: Dull black surfaces absorb most of the radiation falling on them.

questions.stem: A solar panel of area 2.5 m^2 receives sunlight of intensity 800 W/m^2. If its efficiency is 15%, find its electrical power output.
questions.explanation: Incident power = 800 x 2.5 = 2000 W; output = 0.15 x 2000 = 300 W.

questions.stem: A solar collector usually has a glass cover over the absorbing plate in order to
options: trap heat by the greenhouse effect
conduct heat out of the collector
questions.explanation: Glass lets in short-wave solar radiation but blocks the long-wave infrared re-emitted by the warm plate.

questions.stem: In a solar-powered street light, energy collected during the day is stored for use at night in
questions.explanation: The panel charges a battery, which supplies the lamp after dark.

questions.stem: A 25 kg box rests on a horizontal floor. If the coefficient of limiting friction is 0.4, find the least horizontal force needed to start it moving. (g = 10 m/s^2)
A block placed on a plane is just about to slide when the plane is tilted at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Find the coefficient of static friction.
questions.explanation: At the point of slipping, mu = tan(theta) = tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3), about 0.58.

questions.stem: A horizontal force of 60 N pulls a 20 kg crate along a floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Find the acceleration of the crate. (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: Friction = 0.2 x 200 = 40 N; net force = 20 N; a = 20/20 = 1 m/s^2.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of friction?
options: It allows us to walk without slipping
It causes wear and tear of machine parts
It enables car brakes to work
It allows a nail to hold in wood
questions.explanation: Friction between moving parts wastes energy as heat and wears surfaces away.

questions.stem: Friction in moving machine parts can be reduced by
questions.explanation: Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, and lubricants separate surfaces.

questions.stem: A small steel ball falling through glycerine eventually moves with a constant velocity called the terminal velocity. At this stage
options: the weight equals the sum of the upthrust and the viscous drag
the upthrust is greater than the weight
the ball has zero acceleration because its weight is zero
questions.explanation: With no net force the acceleration is zero, so the velocity stays constant.

questions.stem: According to Stokes' law, the viscous force on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid is proportional to the
options: radius and the velocity of the sphere
questions.explanation: F = 6 pi eta r v, so F is proportional to r and v.

questions.stem: Static friction is generally
options: greater than kinetic (dynamic) friction for the same surfaces
questions.explanation: It takes more force to start a body sliding than to keep it sliding.

questions.stem: The limiting frictional force between two surfaces does NOT depend on the
options: area of the surfaces in contact
questions.explanation: One of the laws of solid friction is that limiting friction is independent of the area of contact.

questions.stem: A machine lifts a load of 600 N with an effort of 150 N. Find its mechanical advantage.
questions.explanation: MA = load/effort = 600/150 = 4.

questions.stem: A machine with velocity ratio 5 lifts a load of 600 N when an effort of 150 N is applied. Find its efficiency.
questions.explanation: MA = 4; efficiency = MA/VR x 100% = 4/5 x 100% = 80%.

questions.stem: A pulley system with 4 pulleys has a velocity ratio of 4. If its efficiency is 75%, what effort is needed to raise a load of 300 N?
questions.explanation: MA = efficiency x VR = 0.75 x 4 = 3, so effort = 300/3 = 100 N.

questions.stem: Find the velocity ratio of an inclined plane that makes an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal.
questions.explanation: VR = length of slope/height = 1/sin(theta) = 1/sin 30 = 2.

questions.stem: A screw jack has a pitch of 5 mm and a handle of length 35 cm. Find its velocity ratio.
questions.explanation: VR = 2 pi (handle length)/pitch = 2 pi (350 mm)/5 mm = 140 pi, about 440.

questions.stem: A pair of scissors is an example of a
questions.explanation: The pivot (fulcrum) lies between the effort and the load.

questions.stem: A wheelbarrow is a second class lever because
options: the fulcrum is between the load and the effort
the effort is between the load and the fulcrum
the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
questions.explanation: The wheel is the fulcrum, the load is in the tray, and the effort is at the handles.

questions.stem: The efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100% because
options: the load is always greater than the effort
some of the work input is used to overcome friction and lift moving parts
velocity ratio is less than one
questions.explanation: Work output is always less than input; the difference is wasted mainly through friction.

questions.stem: In a wheel and axle the wheel radius is 50 cm and the axle radius is 10 cm. If the machine is 70% efficient, find the effort needed to lift a 1400 N load.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: A spring stretches by 4 cm under a load of 20 N. How much will it stretch under a load of 35 N, assuming the elastic limit is not exceeded?

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: A spring of force constant 400 N/m is stretched by 5 cm. Find the energy stored in it.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 2 x 10^(-6) m^2 stretches by 0.5 mm under a tension of 100 N. Find Young's modulus of the material.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: The point beyond which a wire does not return to its original length when the load is removed is the
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is permanent (plastic).

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: A spring balance can be marked with a uniform (evenly spaced) scale because
options: the upthrust on the spring is constant
the moments about the hook are balanced
the extension of its spring is proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit
questions.explanation: This is Hooke's law; equal increases in load give equal increases in extension.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: Two identical springs, each of force constant 300 N/m, are joined end to end (in series). Find the force constant of the combination.
questions.explanation: For springs in series 1/k = 1/300 + 1/300, so k = 150 N/m (in parallel it would be 600 N/m).

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: Strain is defined as
options: stress divided by Young's modulus squared
questions.explanation: Strain = e/l and has no unit.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: The unit of Young's modulus is the same as that of
questions.explanation: Young's modulus = stress/strain, and strain has no unit, so its unit is N/m^2 (Pa), like pressure.

questions.topic: Elasticity: Hooke's law and Young's modulus
questions.stem: A load of 40 N stretches an elastic cord by 8 cm within its elastic limit. Find the work done in stretching it.
Find the pressure due to water at a depth of 15 m in a lake. (density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
The height of mercury in a barometer is 76 cm. Calculate the atmospheric pressure. (density of mercury = 13 600 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
A box weighing 600 N rests on a face measuring 0.4 m by 0.25 m. Find the pressure it exerts on the floor.
In a hydraulic press, the small piston has area 0.02 m^2 and the large piston has area 0.5 m^2. If a force of 200 N is applied to the small piston, what force acts on the large piston?
questions.explanation: Pressure is transmitted equally: F = 200 x (0.5/0.02) = 5000 N.

questions.stem: The instrument used to measure the pressure of gas supply is the
questions.explanation: A U-tube manometer compares gas pressure with atmospheric pressure by a liquid level difference.

questions.stem: An aneroid barometer can be used as an altimeter because
options: air density is constant with height
questions.explanation: Readings of pressure can be calibrated in terms of height above sea level.

questions.stem: Water is not used in a simple barometer mainly because
options: the column needed would be about 10 m high
questions.explanation: Water is about 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so atmospheric pressure supports a column of about 10 m.

questions.stem: What height of water column would atmospheric pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa support? (density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
A diver is 20 m below the surface of the sea. If atmospheric pressure is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, find the total pressure on the diver. (density of sea water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: Total pressure = atmospheric + rho g h = 1.0 x 10^5 + 2.0 x 10^5 = 3.0 x 10^5 Pa.

questions.stem: Pressure in a liquid at a given depth
options: depends on the shape of the container
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure at a point is the same in all directions and depends only on depth and density.

questions.stem: A stone weighs 60 N in air and 40 N when completely immersed in water. Find its relative density.
questions.explanation: Upthrust = 60 - 40 = 20 N; relative density = weight in air/loss in weight = 60/20 = 3.

questions.stem: A metal block of volume 5 x 10^(-4) m^3 is fully submerged in water. Find the upthrust on it. (density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = 1000 x 5 x 10^(-4) x 10 = 5 N.

questions.stem: A body weighs 60 N in air, 40 N in water and 44 N in a certain oil. Find the relative density of the oil.
questions.explanation: RD of oil = loss of weight in oil/loss of weight in water = 16/20 = 0.8.

questions.stem: A body floats in a liquid when
options: its weight is greater than the upthrust
its weight equals the weight of liquid it displaces
it displaces its own volume of liquid
its density is greater than that of the liquid
questions.explanation: The law of flotation: a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid.

questions.stem: A block of ice of density 900 kg/m^3 floats in water of density 1000 kg/m^3. What fraction of its volume is below the surface?
questions.explanation: Weight = upthrust gives rho(ice) V = rho(water) V(submerged), so V(submerged)/V = 900/1000 = 9/10.

questions.stem: A hydrometer is used to measure the
questions.explanation: A hydrometer floats deeper in less dense liquids; its stem is graduated in relative density.

questions.stem: A loaded ship sinks deeper when it sails from the sea into a freshwater river because
options: fresh water is denser than sea water
fresh water is less dense than sea water
upthrust is greater in fresh water
questions.explanation: To displace the same weight of a less dense liquid, a larger volume must be displaced.

questions.stem: A solid of mass 270 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 30 cm^3 to 130 cm^3. Find the density of the solid.
A wooden block of volume 0.002 m^3 and density 600 kg/m^3 floats in water. What extra downward force is needed to just submerge it completely? (density of water = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: Full upthrust = 1000 x 0.002 x 10 = 20 N; weight = 600 x 0.002 x 10 = 12 N; extra force = 20 - 12 = 8 N.

questions.stem: Archimedes' principle states that when a body is wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the
questions.explanation: This upthrust explains why bodies appear to lose weight in fluids.

questions.stem: Convert 37 degrees Celsius to the Kelvin scale.
Express 35 degrees Celsius in degrees Fahrenheit.
The mercury thread of an uncalibrated thermometer is 4 cm long at the ice point and 24 cm at the steam point. What temperature corresponds to a length of 13 cm?
questions.explanation: theta = (13 - 4)/(24 - 4) x 100 = 45 degrees C.

questions.stem: A resistance thermometer reads 50 ohms at 0 degrees C and 90 ohms at 100 degrees C. Find the temperature when its resistance is 62 ohms.
Which of the following is NOT a thermometric property?
options: Pressure of a gas at constant volume
questions.explanation: A thermometric property must vary continuously and measurably with temperature; mass does not.

questions.stem: A clinical thermometer has a constriction in its bore in order to
options: prevent the mercury from returning to the bulb before it is read
make it more sensitive to cold
questions.explanation: The constriction breaks the thread, so the maximum reading stays until the thermometer is shaken.

questions.stem: The most suitable thermometer for measuring the temperature of a furnace at about 1500 degrees C is a
questions.explanation: Liquid-in-glass thermometers fail at such temperatures; thermocouples and pyrometers have very high ranges.

questions.stem: Alcohol is preferred to mercury in thermometers used in very cold regions because alcohol
questions.explanation: Mercury freezes at about -39 degrees C, while alcohol freezes at about -115 degrees C.

questions.stem: A steel rail is 50 m long at 20 degrees C. By how much does it expand when heated to 60 degrees C? (linear expansivity of steel = 1.2 x 10^(-5) per K)
questions.explanation: Expansion = alpha L theta = 1.2 x 10^(-5) x 50 x 40 = 0.024 m.

questions.stem: If the linear expansivity of a solid is alpha, its cubic (volume) expansivity is approximately
questions.explanation: Volume expansivity is about three times the linear expansivity; area expansivity is about 2 alpha.

questions.stem: A brass rod 1.5 m long expands by 1.8 mm when heated through 60 K. Find the linear expansivity of brass.
questions.explanation: alpha = extension/(L x theta) = 0.0018/(1.5 x 60) = 2.0 x 10^(-5) per K.

questions.stem: Gaps are left between lengths of railway lines in order to
options: allow for expansion in hot weather
questions.explanation: Without gaps, expansion on hot days would buckle the rails.

questions.stem: A bimetallic strip made of brass and iron bends when heated because
options: brass expands more than iron for the same temperature rise
questions.explanation: Unequal expansion makes the strip curve with the brass on the outside of the curve.

questions.stem: Water has its maximum density at
questions.explanation: Because of the anomalous expansion of water, it contracts from 0 to 4 degrees C and expands above 4 degrees C.

questions.stem: The apparent expansivity of a liquid is less than its real expansivity because
options: heat is lost to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Real expansivity = apparent expansivity + volume expansivity of the container.

questions.stem: A metal plate has an area of 2.0 m^2 at 0 degrees C. Find its area at 100 degrees C if the linear expansivity of the metal is 1.5 x 10^(-5) per K.
questions.explanation: Area expansivity = 2 alpha = 3 x 10^(-5) per K; new area = 2.0(1 + 3 x 10^(-5) x 100) = 2.006 m^2.

questions.stem: Telephone wires are left to sag when fixed during hot weather so that
options: they do not snap when they contract in cold weather
questions.explanation: Wires contract when cold; slack prevents excessive tension.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 600 cm^3 at a pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. Find its volume at 2.5 x 10^5 Pa if the temperature stays constant.
A gas has a volume of 300 cm^3 at 27 degrees C. Find its volume at 87 degrees C if the pressure is constant.
questions.explanation: Charles' law with kelvin temperatures: V2 = 300 x 360/300 = 360 cm^3. Using Celsius values gives the wrong answer 967 cm^3.

questions.stem: A sealed gas cylinder is at a pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa at 27 degrees C. At what temperature will the pressure be 1.5 x 10^5 Pa?
questions.explanation: P/T is constant: T2 = 1.5 x 300 = 450 K = 177 degrees C.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 50 cm^3 at 2 x 10^5 Pa and 27 degrees C. Find its volume at 1 x 10^5 Pa and 127 degrees C.
Absolute zero of temperature is
questions.explanation: Absolute zero, 0 K, corresponds to about -273 degrees C.

questions.stem: A container of volume 0.03 m^3 holds an ideal gas at 8.3 x 10^5 Pa and 300 K. How many moles of gas does it contain? (R = 8.3 J/(mol K))
A graph of pressure against 1/volume for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is
options: a straight line through the origin
a straight line with a negative slope
questions.explanation: Boyle's law gives P = k(1/V), which is a straight line through the origin.

questions.stem: Van der Waals modified the ideal gas equation to allow for
options: the speed of sound in the gas
the volume of the molecules and the forces between them
questions.explanation: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour because molecules have finite size and attract one another.

questions.stem: Boyle's law relates the pressure and volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant
questions.explanation: Boyle's law is an isothermal relationship: PV = constant.

questions.stem: Charles' law is described as an isobaric process because the
questions.explanation: Isobaric means constant pressure; V/T is then constant.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 25 degrees C to 75 degrees C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg K))
Water of mass 0.2 kg at 80 degrees C is mixed with 0.3 kg of water at 20 degrees C. Assuming no heat loss, find the final temperature.
questions.explanation: Heat lost = heat gained: 0.2(80 - T) = 0.3(T - 20), so T = 44 degrees C.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg metal block at 100 degrees C is dropped into 0.4 kg of water at 20 degrees C. The final temperature is 30 degrees C. Find the specific heat capacity of the metal. (c of water = 4200 J/(kg K); neglect heat losses)
A 2000 W electric kettle heats 1.5 kg of water from 20 degrees C to 100 degrees C. Assuming no heat loss, how long does this take? (c of water = 4200 J/(kg K))
The heat capacity of a body is the heat required to
options: raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K
raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 K
change 1 kg of it into vapour
questions.explanation: Heat capacity = mass x specific heat capacity (unit J/K).

questions.stem: Find the heat capacity of an iron pot of mass 0.8 kg. (specific heat capacity of iron = 450 J/(kg K))
Coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas mainly because water has a
questions.explanation: Water warms up and cools down slowly, moderating nearby land temperatures.

questions.stem: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of heat loss of a body is proportional to the
options: excess of its temperature over that of its surroundings
questions.explanation: This holds approximately for small temperature differences with forced convection.

questions.stem: A 1000 W immersion heater, 84% efficient, is placed in 2 kg of water for 1 minute. Find the rise in temperature of the water. (c of water = 4200 J/(kg K))
Water falls 84 m over a waterfall. If all its potential energy becomes heat in the water, find the rise in temperature. (c = 4200 J/(kg K), g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: mgh = mc(theta), so theta = gh/c = 10 x 84/4200 = 0.2 K.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degrees C? (specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 000 J/kg)
Find the heat needed to change 0.2 kg of ice at 0 degrees C into water at 40 degrees C. (latent heat of fusion = 336 000 J/kg, c of water = 4200 J/(kg K))
An electric heater of power 500 W boils off 0.05 kg of water at 100 degrees C in 4 minutes. Find the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water from these results.
During melting, the temperature of a pure solid
options: remains constant until all of it has melted
questions.explanation: The heat supplied (latent heat) breaks the bonds between molecules rather than raising their kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Increasing the pressure on the surface of water
options: has no effect on its boiling point
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs when the saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure; higher pressure needs a higher temperature (the principle of the pressure cooker).

questions.stem: Adding salt to ice
options: does not affect its melting point
raises the boiling point of the ice
questions.explanation: Dissolved impurities lower the melting point, which is why salt is used to de-ice roads.

questions.stem: Evaporation differs from boiling in that evaporation
options: takes place at a fixed temperature
takes place at all temperatures and only at the surface
questions.explanation: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a definite temperature; evaporation is a surface process at any temperature.

questions.stem: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because
options: the boiling point of water is lowered
the boiling point of water is raised by the increased pressure
steam conducts heat better than water
the food absorbs latent heat of fusion
questions.explanation: At higher pressure water boils above 100 degrees C, so food is cooked at a higher temperature.

questions.stem: Sweating cools the body because
options: sweat is colder than the body
evaporation of sweat absorbs latent heat from the skin
questions.explanation: Evaporation requires latent heat of vaporisation, taken from the skin.

questions.stem: Water boils below 100 degrees C at the top of a high mountain because
options: there is less oxygen to support boiling
the atmospheric pressure is lower, so the saturated vapour pressure equals it at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A liquid boils when its S.V.P. equals the external pressure; lower external pressure means a lower boiling point.

questions.stem: The saturated vapour pressure of a liquid depends only on its
questions.explanation: S.V.P. increases with temperature and is independent of the volume of vapour space (unlike an unsaturated vapour).

questions.stem: On a clear night, dew forms on grass when the air in contact with the grass is cooled to
options: the temperature at which the air becomes saturated with water vapour
the temperature of maximum density of water
the boiling point of water at that pressure
questions.explanation: That temperature is the dew point: further cooling makes the excess vapour condense as dew.

questions.stem: A wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer is used to determine
questions.explanation: The difference between wet- and dry-bulb readings, with tables, gives the relative humidity.

questions.stem: The vapour pressure of water in the air is 1.6 kPa and the saturated vapour pressure at the air temperature is 2.0 kPa. Find the relative humidity.
questions.explanation: RH = actual vapour pressure/S.V.P. x 100% = 1.6/2.0 x 100% = 80%.

questions.stem: When the wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometers of a hygrometer show the same reading, the relative humidity is
questions.explanation: No evaporation occurs from the wet bulb when the air is already saturated.

questions.stem: An unsaturated vapour behaves approximately like
options: a saturated vapour with constant pressure
an ideal gas obeying Boyle's law
questions.explanation: An unsaturated vapour obeys the gas laws approximately; a saturated vapour does not.

questions.stem: Brownian motion of pollen grains in water provides evidence that
options: water molecules are in constant random motion
questions.explanation: Uneven bombardment by moving water molecules jerks the grains about.

questions.stem: A needle can float on the surface of clean water because of
questions.explanation: The surface behaves like a stretched elastic skin that can support the small weight.

questions.stem: Water rises in a narrow glass tube but mercury is depressed because
options: water evaporates and mercury does not
adhesion between water and glass exceeds cohesion of water, while cohesion of mercury exceeds its adhesion to glass
questions.explanation: The balance of adhesive and cohesive forces decides whether a liquid wets glass and the direction of capillary movement.

questions.stem: Adding detergent to water
questions.explanation: Detergents lower surface tension, helping water spread and wet fabrics.

questions.stem: The angle of contact between pure water and clean glass is
questions.explanation: Water wets clean glass completely; mercury has an obtuse angle of contact (about 140 degrees).

questions.stem: The rate of diffusion of a gas is increased by
options: increasing the mass of its molecules
increasing the pressure of a heavier surrounding gas
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means faster-moving molecules, so they spread out more quickly.

questions.stem: The force of attraction between molecules of the same substance is called
questions.explanation: Adhesion is attraction between molecules of different substances.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by a gas is due to
options: the gas molecules being at rest
collisions of its molecules with the walls of the container
questions.explanation: Each collision transfers momentum, and the rate of change of momentum per unit area is the pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic theory of gases?
options: Collisions between molecules are perfectly elastic
Molecules occupy most of the volume of the gas
Molecules move only in straight lines towards the walls
questions.explanation: The simple theory assumes elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume and no intermolecular forces except during collisions.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, raising the temperature of a gas
options: increases the mass of each molecule
increases the average kinetic energy of its molecules
questions.explanation: Absolute temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

questions.stem: Kinetic theory explains Boyle's law by stating that when the volume of a gas is halved at constant temperature
options: molecules hit the walls twice as often, doubling the pressure
questions.explanation: The same molecules with the same average speed strike a smaller area more often.

questions.stem: If the absolute temperature of a gas is increased by a factor of 4, the root mean square speed of its molecules
questions.explanation: Mean kinetic energy (proportional to v^2) is proportional to T, so v(rms) is proportional to sqrt(T); sqrt(4) = 2.

questions.stem: Evaporation causes cooling of the remaining liquid because
options: the faster-moving molecules escape, lowering the average kinetic energy
the liquid gains heat from the air
questions.explanation: Losing the most energetic molecules reduces the average energy, hence the temperature.

questions.stem: Heat from the sun reaches the earth mainly by
questions.explanation: Space is nearly a vacuum, and only radiation can cross a vacuum.

questions.stem: In a vacuum flask, which feature mainly reduces heat transfer by radiation?
options: The narrow neck of the flask
The silvered surfaces of the double walls
questions.explanation: Shiny silvered surfaces are poor emitters and good reflectors of radiation; the vacuum stops conduction and convection.

questions.stem: Land breeze blows from land to sea at night because
options: the sea cools faster than the land
the land is warmer than the sea at night
the land cools faster than the sea, so the warmer air over the sea rises
sea air is denser at night
questions.explanation: Water has a higher specific heat capacity and stays warmer at night; air rises over it and cooler land air flows out to replace it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals such as copper conduct heat well because of their free electrons.

questions.stem: A copper plate of area 0.02 m^2 and thickness 5 mm has its faces at temperatures differing by 50 K. Find the rate of heat flow through it. (thermal conductivity of copper = 400 W/(m K))
Overhead water tanks on rooftops are often painted white or silver so that the water stays cool, because such surfaces
options: absorb more radiation than dark surfaces
reflect most of the radiation falling on them
set up convection currents in the water
questions.explanation: Light, shiny surfaces are poor absorbers and good reflectors of radiant heat from the sun.

questions.stem: Temperature gradient in a conductor is defined as the
options: temperature difference per unit length along the conductor
questions.explanation: Temperature gradient = (theta1 - theta2)/x, in K/m.

questions.stem: The heating element of an electric kettle is placed near the bottom so that
options: convection currents can heat all the water
the water boils only at the top
questions.explanation: Warm water rises and cold water sinks, circulating heat through the kettle.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 40 cm. Find its speed.
questions.explanation: v = f x wavelength = 50 x 0.4 = 20 m/s.

questions.stem: Water waves on a lake have a wavelength of 80 m and travel at 20 m/s. Find their period.
questions.explanation: T = wavelength/v = 80/20 = 4 s.

questions.stem: A wave transfers
options: matter from the source to the receiver
energy from one point to another without net transfer of the medium
questions.explanation: Particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions while energy travels along.

questions.stem: A progressive wave is described by y = 0.05 sin 2 pi(100t - 2.5x), with x and y in metres and t in seconds. Find the speed of the wave.
questions.explanation: Comparing with y = A sin 2 pi(ft - x/wavelength): f = 100 Hz and wavelength = 1/2.5 = 0.4 m, so v = 40 m/s.

questions.stem: For the wave y = 0.05 sin 2 pi(100t - 2.5x) (SI units), what is the amplitude?
questions.explanation: The amplitude is the coefficient of the sine function, 0.05 m.

questions.stem: Two points on a progressive wave are 15 cm apart. If the wavelength is 60 cm, find the phase difference between them.
questions.explanation: Phase difference = 2 pi x/wavelength = 2 pi (15/60) = pi/2 radians.

questions.stem: A vibrating source completes one oscillation every 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
options: Wave on a plucked guitar string
questions.explanation: In sound waves the air particles vibrate along the direction the wave travels.

questions.stem: Which of the following waves can travel through a vacuum?
questions.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic and need no material medium; mechanical waves do.

questions.stem: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate
options: parallel to the direction of propagation
at right angles to the direction of propagation
in the same direction at all points
questions.explanation: Ripples on water and waves on strings are transverse.

questions.stem: A stationary wave differs from a progressive wave in that it
options: has nodes and antinodes and does not transfer energy along the medium
travels faster than a progressive wave
questions.explanation: A stationary wave is formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; energy is stored, not transmitted.

questions.stem: The distance between two adjacent nodes of a stationary wave is 30 cm. What is the wavelength?
questions.explanation: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the wavelength is 2 x 30 = 60 cm.

questions.stem: Which of the following waves can be polarised?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

questions.stem: The bending of waves round the edges of an obstacle is called
questions.explanation: Diffraction is greatest when the gap or obstacle is comparable in size to the wavelength.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties shows that light waves are transverse?
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised, so polarisation proves light is transverse.

questions.stem: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. Find the beat frequency.
questions.explanation: Beat frequency = difference in frequencies = 260 - 256 = 4 Hz.

questions.stem: A tuning fork of 384 Hz produces 6 beats per second with a guitar string. When the string is tightened slightly the beats decrease. What was the original frequency of the string?
questions.explanation: The string was 384 +/- 6 Hz; tightening raises its frequency, and the beats fall only if it moves towards 384, so it was 378 Hz.

questions.stem: The apparent change in frequency of a sound when the source moves relative to the listener is known as the
questions.explanation: An approaching source sounds higher in pitch and a receding one lower.

questions.stem: When water waves pass from deep water to shallow water, which of the following remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength decrease in shallow water.

questions.stem: Interference of two waves is constructive at a point when their path difference is
options: an odd number of half wavelengths
questions.explanation: Crests then meet crests, giving maximum amplitude.

questions.stem: As the siren of an ambulance approaches and then passes a stationary observer, the pitch heard
options: is higher while approaching and falls as it moves away
is lower while approaching and rises as it moves away
questions.explanation: Waves are crowded together in front of a moving source (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) and spread out behind it.

questions.stem: Sound cannot travel through
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium.

questions.stem: In which of the following does sound travel fastest?
options: Hydrogen gas at the same temperature
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

questions.stem: A girl claps her hands in front of a cliff and hears the echo 1.5 s later. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
questions.explanation: The sound travels to the cliff and back: 2d = 340 x 1.5, so d = 255 m.

questions.stem: A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse to the sea bed and receives the echo 0.6 s later. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, find the depth of the sea.
Thunder is heard 3 s after a lightning flash is seen. How far away is the storm? (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: Light arrives almost instantly, so distance = 340 x 3 = 1020 m.

questions.stem: Reverberation in a large hall can be reduced by
options: covering the walls with soft, absorbent materials
questions.explanation: Soft materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it repeatedly.

questions.stem: The speed of sound in air increases when the
questions.explanation: v is proportional to sqrt(T); at constant temperature pressure has no effect.

questions.stem: A man standing between two cliffs fires a gun and hears the first echo after 2 s and the second after 3 s. If the speed of sound is 330 m/s, find the distance between the cliffs.
questions.explanation: Distances to the cliffs are 330 x 2/2 = 330 m and 330 x 3/2 = 495 m; total = 825 m.

questions.stem: The pitch of a note depends mainly on its
questions.explanation: Higher frequency gives a higher pitch.

questions.stem: The loudness of a sound depends mainly on its
questions.explanation: Loudness is related to intensity, which depends on the square of the amplitude.

questions.stem: Two musical instruments playing the same note can be distinguished by their
questions.explanation: Different instruments produce different overtones, giving each a distinct quality.

questions.stem: Find the fundamental frequency of a pipe 25 cm long closed at one end. (speed of sound = 330 m/s; neglect end correction)
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe L = wavelength/4, so f = v/(4L) = 330/1 = 330 Hz.

questions.stem: Find the fundamental frequency of a pipe 50 cm long open at both ends. (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
questions.explanation: For an open pipe L = wavelength/2, so f = v/(2L) = 340/1 = 340 Hz.

questions.stem: A string 80 cm long with mass per unit length 0.01 kg/m is stretched by a tension of 64 N. Find its fundamental frequency.
If the tension in a stretched string is increased four times while the length stays the same, its fundamental frequency is
questions.explanation: f is proportional to sqrt(T), and sqrt(4) = 2.

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 120 Hz. Which of the following is a possible overtone of this pipe?
questions.explanation: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: 120, 360, 600, 840 Hz, ...; 240, 480 and 720 Hz are even harmonics.

questions.stem: A tuning fork of 500 Hz is held over a resonance tube closed at the bottom by water. Find the shortest air column that resonates. (speed of sound = 340 m/s; neglect end correction)
questions.explanation: The first resonance occurs at L = wavelength/4 = (340/500)/4 = 0.17 m = 17 cm; the next is at 3/4 wavelength = 51 cm.

questions.stem: A tuning fork is said to produce a pure tone because it
options: vibrates mainly at one frequency with almost no overtones
questions.explanation: A pure tone contains only the fundamental frequency.

questions.stem: Resonance occurs when
options: a body is made to vibrate at its own natural frequency by a periodic force
a wave is reflected from a hard surface
the amplitude of a vibration is zero
questions.explanation: At resonance energy is transferred most efficiently, giving a large amplitude.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a luminous object?
questions.explanation: Luminous bodies produce their own light; the moon only reflects sunlight.

questions.stem: The formation of shadows is evidence that light
questions.explanation: Rectilinear propagation explains sharp shadows of opaque objects.

questions.stem: Which arrangement of the sun, earth and moon, in a straight line, gives an eclipse of the moon (lunar eclipse)?
options: Sun, moon, earth, with the moon in the middle
Earth, sun, moon, with the sun in the middle
Sun, earth, moon, with the earth in the middle
Any arrangement, provided it is night time
questions.explanation: The moon is darkened when it passes into the earth's shadow, which needs the earth between the sun and the moon.

questions.stem: A pinhole camera is 12 cm long. It forms an image of a tree 8 m away. If the image is 2.4 cm tall, how tall is the tree?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image distance/object distance = 0.12/8 = 0.015, so tree height = 0.024/0.015 = 1.6 m.

questions.stem: The image formed in a pinhole camera is
questions.explanation: Rays cross at the pinhole, so the image on the screen is inverted, and it is real because it forms on a screen.

questions.stem: Making the pinhole of a pinhole camera larger makes the image
questions.explanation: A larger hole lets in more light, but each point of the object gives a larger patch on the screen.

questions.stem: The sun is about 1.5 x 10^11 m from the earth. How long does sunlight take to reach the earth? (c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s)
questions.explanation: t = distance/speed = 1.5 x 10^11/(3.0 x 10^8) = 500 s (about 8 minutes).

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at a glancing angle of 35 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: The glancing angle is measured from the mirror, so the angle of incidence (from the normal) is 55 degrees, and reflection equals incidence.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: How many images are formed of an object placed between two plane mirrors inclined at 60 degrees?

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A plane mirror is rotated through 12 degrees while the incident ray stays fixed. Through what angle does the reflected ray turn?
questions.explanation: Rotating a mirror through theta turns the reflected ray through 2 theta.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the linear magnification of the image.
questions.explanation: m = v/u = 30/15 = 2; the real image is twice the size of the object.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is 30 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image formed?
options: 60 cm in front of the mirror (real)
12 cm in front of the mirror (real)
questions.explanation: With the real-is-positive convention f = -20 cm: 1/v = -1/20 - 1/30 = -1/12, so v = -12 cm, i.e. a virtual image 12 cm behind the mirror.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Convex mirrors are used as driving mirrors because they
options: give a wide field of view and upright images
questions.explanation: The diminished, upright, virtual image covers a wide area behind the vehicle.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Concave mirrors are used in car headlamps with the bulb placed at the principal focus so that
options: a parallel beam of light is produced
an image of the bulb forms on the road
questions.explanation: Rays from the focus are reflected parallel to the principal axis.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: The radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 36 cm. Its focal length is

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: The image formed by a plane mirror is
options: virtual, inverted and the same size
questions.explanation: It is the same size as the object and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A girl walks towards a plane mirror at 2 m/s. At what rate does she approach her image?
questions.explanation: The image moves towards the mirror at 2 m/s as well, so the separation closes at 4 m/s.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A ray in air strikes a glass surface at an angle of incidence of 45 degrees. If the refractive index of the glass is sqrt(2), find the angle of refraction.
questions.explanation: sin r = sin 45/sqrt(2) = (1/sqrt(2))/sqrt(2) = 1/2, so r = 30 degrees.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Find the critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.
questions.explanation: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = 41.8 degrees.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A coin at the bottom of a tank of water 2.4 m deep appears to be 1.8 m below the surface. Find the refractive index of water.
questions.explanation: n = real depth/apparent depth = 2.4/1.8 = 4/3.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A mark is viewed vertically through a glass block 9 cm thick of refractive index 1.5. By how much is the mark apparently raised?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = 9/1.5 = 6 cm, so the mark appears raised by 9 - 6 = 3 cm.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Find the speed of light in glass of refractive index 1.5. (c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s)

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from
options: a less dense to a denser medium at any angle
a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
air into glass at a small angle
a denser to a less dense medium at a small angle
questions.explanation: Both conditions must hold: optically denser to less dense, and incidence beyond the critical angle.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: Optical fibres used in telecommunication depend on
questions.explanation: Light is trapped in the core by repeated total internal reflections.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is placed 20 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the position of the image.
options: 60 cm on the other side of the lens

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the height of the image.
questions.explanation: v = 15 cm, magnification = 15/30 = 0.5, so the image is 2 cm tall.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: A prism of refracting angle 60 degrees gives a minimum deviation of 40 degrees. Find its refractive index.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane and curved surfaces
questions.stem: The power of a converging lens of focal length 25 cm is
questions.explanation: P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.25 = +4 dioptres.

questions.stem: Short sight (myopia) is corrected by using a
questions.explanation: The diverging lens makes rays from distant objects appear to come from the far point of the eye.

questions.stem: Long sight (hypermetropia) is corrected by using a
questions.explanation: A converging lens brings near objects to focus on the retina.

questions.stem: A long-sighted man has a near point of 75 cm. What lens does he need to read a book held 25 cm from his eye?
options: diverging lens of focal length 37.5 cm
converging lens of focal length 37.5 cm
converging lens of focal length 18.75 cm
diverging lens of focal length 75 cm
questions.explanation: The lens must form a virtual image at 75 cm of an object at 25 cm: 1/f = 1/25 - 1/75, so f = +37.5 cm.

questions.stem: A short-sighted girl has a far point of 2 m. Find the power of the lens she needs to see distant objects clearly.
questions.explanation: She needs a diverging lens with f = -2 m (image of a distant object at her far point); P = 1/f = -0.5 D.

questions.stem: In a compound microscope the final image is
questions.explanation: The objective forms a real inverted image, which the eyepiece magnifies as a virtual image.

questions.stem: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4 cm. Find its angular magnification.
questions.explanation: M = f(objective)/f(eyepiece) = 100/4 = 25; the tube length would be 104 cm.

questions.stem: In the camera, the part that corresponds to the retina of the eye is the
questions.explanation: The image is focused onto the film (or sensor), just as the eye focuses onto the retina.

questions.stem: The camera focuses objects at different distances by
options: changing the focal length of the lens
changing the distance between the lens and the film
changing the size of the aperture
questions.explanation: In the eye the focal length changes (accommodation), but in a simple camera the lens moves.

questions.stem: A magnifying glass of focal length 5 cm forms a virtual image at the near point (25 cm). Find its magnifying power.
A projector forms on the screen an image that is
questions.explanation: The slide is placed just beyond the focal point of the projection lens, giving a large real image; the slide is inserted upside down so the picture appears upright.

questions.stem: The separation of white light into its component colours by a prism is called
questions.explanation: Different colours have different refractive indices in glass, so they are refracted by different amounts.

questions.stem: Which colour of light is deviated most by a glass prism?
questions.explanation: Violet has the highest refractive index in glass and is bent the most.

questions.stem: Mixing red, green and blue light in the right proportions on a white screen produces
questions.explanation: Red, green and blue are the additive primary colours.

questions.stem: A red rose viewed in pure blue light appears
questions.explanation: The red petals absorb blue light and there is no red light to reflect, so they look black.

questions.stem: A rainbow is formed by
options: refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops
questions.explanation: Each drop refracts and disperses sunlight and reflects it internally back towards the observer.

questions.stem: Yellow light can be produced by adding
questions.explanation: In additive mixing, red + green = yellow; red + blue = magenta; blue + green = cyan.

questions.stem: Which of the following combinations of paints (subtractive mixing) gives green?
questions.explanation: Yellow paint reflects red and green; cyan reflects green and blue; only green is reflected by both.

questions.stem: Which of the following electromagnetic radiations has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: In order of increasing wavelength: gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio.

questions.stem: Which radiation is used in television remote controls?
questions.explanation: Remote controls send coded pulses of infrared radiation.

questions.stem: Ultraviolet radiation can be detected by
options: a thermometer with a blackened bulb
questions.explanation: UV makes fluorescent substances glow; infrared is detected with a blackened thermometer or thermopile.

questions.stem: A radio station broadcasts on a frequency of 150 MHz. Find the wavelength of the waves. (c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s)
Which electromagnetic radiation is used to sterilise surgical instruments and to treat cancer?
questions.explanation: High-energy gamma rays kill bacteria and cancer cells.

questions.stem: All electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum with the same
questions.explanation: They all travel at c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum.

questions.stem: Microwave ovens cook food mainly because microwaves
options: are reflected by water in the food
are absorbed by water molecules in the food
questions.explanation: Water molecules absorb microwave energy and vibrate faster, heating the food.

questions.stem: Two point charges of 2 microcoulombs and 3 microcoulombs are 30 cm apart in air. Find the force between them. (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^(-2))
If the distance between two point charges is halved, the force between them becomes
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law: F is proportional to 1/r^2, and (1/(1/2))^2 = 4.

questions.stem: Find the electric field intensity 20 cm from a point charge of 4 nC in air. (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^(-2))
How much work is done in moving a charge of 5 microcoulombs through a potential difference of 200 V?
When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the rod becomes positively charged because
options: protons move from the silk to the rod
electrons move from the silk to the rod
electrons are transferred from the rod to the silk
questions.explanation: Only electrons move during charging by friction; losing electrons leaves the rod positive.

questions.stem: The leaves of a positively charged electroscope diverge further when a charged rod is brought near the cap. The rod is
questions.explanation: The positive rod attracts electrons up towards the cap, leaving the leaves more positively charged, so they diverge further; a negative rod would make them collapse first.

questions.stem: A lightning conductor protects a building by
options: storing the charge from the clouds
providing a low-resistance path for charge to flow safely to earth
insulating the building from the ground
questions.explanation: Its sharp points also discharge the air nearby, reducing the chance of a strike.

questions.stem: Find the electric potential at a point 15 cm from a point charge of +5 nC. (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^(-2))
Charge tends to concentrate at the sharp points of a charged conductor because
options: the surface charge density is greatest where the curvature is greatest
questions.explanation: High charge density at points produces strong fields that can ionise the air (point action).

questions.stem: A 20 microfarad capacitor is connected across a 12 V battery. Find the charge stored.
Capacitors of 6 microfarads and 3 microfarads are connected in series. Find the effective capacitance.
questions.explanation: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so C = 2 microfarads. Adding them (9) applies only in parallel.

questions.stem: Two 6 microfarad capacitors in series are connected in parallel with a 4 microfarad capacitor. Find the total capacitance.
questions.explanation: The series pair gives 3 microfarads; adding 4 in parallel gives 7 microfarads.

questions.stem: Find the energy stored in a 50 microfarad capacitor charged to 200 V.
A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.02 m^2 separated by 1 mm of air. Find its capacitance. (permittivity of free space = 8.85 x 10^(-12) F/m)
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor can be increased by
options: reducing the separation of the plates
reducing the area of the plates
increasing the separation of the plates
questions.explanation: C = epsilon A/d, so C rises as d falls, A rises or the permittivity of the dielectric rises.

questions.stem: The SI unit of capacitance is the
questions.explanation: 1 farad = 1 coulomb per volt.

questions.stem: If the voltage across a capacitor is doubled, the energy stored becomes
questions.explanation: E = (1/2)CV^2 is proportional to V^2.

questions.stem: Three 3 microfarad capacitors are connected in parallel across a 10 V supply. Find the total charge stored.
questions.explanation: In parallel C = 9 microfarads, so Q = 9 x 10^(-6) x 10 = 9.0 x 10^(-5) C.

questions.stem: The two main defects of a simple voltaic cell are
options: evaporation and corrosion of the casing
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bubbles on the copper plate cause polarisation; impurities in zinc cause local action.

questions.stem: In a Leclanche cell, polarisation is reduced by
questions.explanation: Manganese(IV) oxide oxidises the hydrogen formed at the carbon rod to water.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a secondary (rechargeable) cell?
questions.explanation: A lead-acid accumulator can be recharged by passing current through it in the reverse direction.

questions.stem: Six cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.2 ohm, are connected in series. Find the total e.m.f. and internal resistance.
questions.explanation: In series the e.m.f.s and the internal resistances add: 6 x 1.5 = 9.0 V and 6 x 0.2 = 1.2 ohm.

questions.stem: Four identical cells, each of e.m.f. 2 V and internal resistance 0.6 ohm, are connected in parallel. Find the e.m.f. and internal resistance of the combination.
questions.explanation: Identical cells in parallel keep the e.m.f. of one cell, while the internal resistance is divided by 4.

questions.stem: A lead-acid accumulator should not be left discharged for a long time because
options: its acid turns to water instantly
questions.explanation: White lead sulphate forms on the plates and is difficult to reverse.

questions.stem: Lithium-ion cells are widely used in mobile phones because they
options: are rechargeable and store much energy for their mass
questions.explanation: Their high energy density and rechargeability suit portable electronics.

questions.stem: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a 4 ohm resistor. Find the current.
A 4 ohm resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors. Find the total resistance.
questions.explanation: The parallel pair gives 6 x 3/(6 + 3) = 2 ohms; adding 4 ohms gives 6 ohms.

questions.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohm is connected to a 2.5 ohm resistor. Find the current.
A cell of e.m.f. 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohm is connected to a 2.5 ohm resistor. Find the terminal p.d. of the cell.
questions.explanation: I = 2 A, so the terminal p.d. = IR = 2 x 2.5 = 5 V; the lost volts are 1 V.

questions.stem: The terminal p.d. of a battery of e.m.f. 3.0 V falls to 2.4 V when it supplies a current of 0.6 A. Find its internal resistance.
questions.explanation: Lost volts = 0.6 V, so r = 0.6/0.6 = 1 ohm.

questions.stem: Find the resistance of a copper wire 100 m long with cross-sectional area 1.0 x 10^(-6) m^2. (resistivity of copper = 1.7 x 10^(-8) ohm m)
A wire of resistance 8 ohms is stretched uniformly to twice its original length. Find its new resistance.
questions.explanation: Doubling the length halves the area (volume is constant), so R = rho L/A becomes 2 x 2 = 4 times larger: 32 ohms.
